one-categorical-displays-s1.title: Favorite kind of film
one-categorical-displays-s1.text: A random sample of 200 teens in a county named their favorite kind of film. "Docs" stands for documentaries (invented data).

plot.label: Bar chart of the relative frequency of each favorite kind of film among 200 teens: comedy 0.30, action 0.25, drama 0.15, horror 0.12, documentaries 0.08, other 0.10

one-categorical-displays-s2.title: A bar chart from a school report
one-categorical-displays-s2.html: A report shows the percent of students who passed a state exam at two schools: 52% at school A and 58% at school B. Its bar chart is below.

items.q: Which kind of film did 15% of the teens choose?

why.correct: Read the height of each bar on the relative frequency axis: drama is at 0.15.
options: The horror bar reaches 0.12, so 12% chose horror.
Right: the drama bar reaches 0.15, which is 15%.
The other bar reaches 0.10, so 10% chose another kind.
The action bar reaches 0.25, so 25% chose action.
Horror, the bar just to the right of drama
Drama
Other, the last bar in the chart
Action, the second bar from the left

items.q: How many of the 200 teens chose action films?

options: The bar shows a relative frequency, 0.25. Multiply by the total, 200.
That is comedy: 0.30 × 200 = 60.
A count from a relative frequency is a multiplication: 0.25 × 200.
Right: $0.25 \times 200 = 50$ teens.
25, reading the bar height as a count
60, which is the number who chose comedy
800, from dividing 200 by 0.25

items.q: Which claim does the bar chart support?

why.correct: Compare bar heights: comedy at 0.30 is twice drama at 0.15. "Most" would need more than 0.50.
options: Right: 0.30 is twice 0.15.
Comedy is the most common choice, but 0.30 is less than half, so not most.
The chart shows how many teens chose each kind as a favorite, not each teen’s ranking of all kinds.
Horror is 0.12, and documentaries plus other is 0.08 + 0.10 = 0.18.
Comedy was chosen about twice as often as drama
Most of the teens in the sample chose comedy as their favorite
Action films are better liked than drama films by each teen
More teens chose horror than chose documentaries and other together

items.q: Could these data also be shown in a pie chart?

why.correct: A pie chart works when every individual is in exactly one category, so the parts add to the whole. Here they add to 1.
options: A pie chart can have many slices; what it needs is parts that make up one whole.
A pie chart shows each category as a part of the whole, which is exactly a relative frequency.
Right: 0.30 + 0.25 + 0.15 + 0.12 + 0.08 + 0.10 = 1, so the slices make one whole.
Sorting is a design choice; the parts already make up one whole.
No: a pie chart can show four categories or fewer
No: pie charts are used for counts, and these are relative frequencies
Yes: each teen chose one kind, so the six parts add to 1
Yes, but just after the bars are sorted from tallest to shortest

items.q: Why does this bar chart give a misleading picture?

why.correct: A bar’s height (or length) must be its value, measured from 0. Starting the axis at 50% exaggerates the difference.
options: Colors help tell the bars apart; they do not change the heights.
Percents are the right choice for schools of different sizes.
Right: with the bottom cut off, bar heights no longer match the values they stand for.
The order of categories in a bar chart is a free choice.
It uses different colors for the two schools’ bars
It shows percents instead of numbers of students passing
Its vertical axis starts at 50%, not at 0%
It puts school A on the left and school B on the right

items.q: In this chart, how many times as tall does school B’s bar look compared with school A’s?

why.correct: The visible heights are $58 - 50 = 8$ and $52 - 50 = 2$, so B looks $\frac{8}{2} = 4$ times as tall, though 58% is only about 1.1 times 52%.
options: Right: above 50%, school A’s bar is 2 points tall and school B’s is 8, a ratio of 4.
That is how the actual percents compare. The drawn bars start at 50, so they look 8/2 = 4 times as tall.
6 is the difference in percents, not the ratio of the drawn heights.
The bars are drawn to different heights: 2 and 8 points above the axis.
4 times
About 1.1 times, as 58 divided by 52
6 times, from the 6 point gap between 58 and 52
The same height, because each bar stands for one school

items.q: Which sentence describes the data honestly?

why.correct: Describe the values themselves: 52% against 58%, a difference of 6 percentage points.
options: That is how the cut-off bars look, not what the percents say.
More than half (52%) of school A’s students passed.
The chart gives percents, not counts; school A could be larger.
Right: 58% − 52% = 6 percentage points, a modest difference.
School B’s pass rate is about four times school A’s rate
Almost no students at school A passed the state exam
School B had more students pass the exam than school A did
School B’s pass rate is 6 points higher than A’s

items.q: How should the chart be redrawn so that bar heights are fair?

why.correct: In a bar chart, heights are compared from 0, so the axis must start at 0.
options: Changing widths adds a second distortion; bar widths should be equal.
Right: then each bar’s height is its percent, and B looks only slightly taller than A.
The two percents are not parts of one whole, so a pie chart does not fit.
Without labels a reader cannot read the values at all.
Make school B’s bar wider than school A’s bar
Start the vertical axis at 0%
Turn it into a pie chart with one slice for each school
Remove the percent labels from the vertical axis

items.q: Which display is made for one categorical variable?

why.correct: Bar charts and pie charts display one categorical variable.
options: Right: one bar per category, with height equal to the count or relative frequency.
A line graph follows a quantity over time, a different situation.
A number line shows numerical values; categories have no positions on a number line.
A list of raw data is not a display; it has not been summarized.
A bar chart
A line graph of the counts over time, day by day
A number line with a mark for each value of the data
A list of each individual in the order they were asked

items.q: A survey asked 300 students, "Which school clubs do you belong to? Check every one." Why is a pie chart a poor choice for the results?

why.correct: A pie chart needs categories that do not overlap and together cover everyone. "Check every one" breaks that.
options: A pie chart shows parts of a whole, which are relative frequencies.
A pie chart can have few or many slices.
Right: the relative frequencies can add to more than 1, so there is no single pie to cut.
Pie charts are for categorical variables; the issue here is overlap.
Pie charts are allowed for counts and not for relative frequencies
There are too few clubs at the school to fill a pie chart
Students can be in several clubs, so the parts do not make one whole
Pie charts are used for quantitative variables such as height

items.q: In a bar chart of favorite fruit, can the bars be put in any order?

why.correct: Categories have no numerical order, so the order of bars is a free choice; sorting by height often helps.
options: Alphabetical order is one choice among many.
Right: many people sort bars by height to make comparisons easier, but any order is correct.
Bars in a bar chart are separated by gaps, and collection order does not matter.
There is no rule about the tallest bar; any order of categories is fine.
No: bars go in alphabetical order so readers can find them
Yes: categories have no number order, so any order works
No: the bars touch, in the order the data were collected
Yes, as long as the tallest bar is placed exactly in the middle

items.q: Two bar charts show favorite subject at a school with 900 students and at a school with 300. Each shows counts. Why is comparing them misleading?

why.correct: To compare groups of different sizes, graph relative frequencies, not counts.
options: They can be compared, once both show relative frequencies.
That limits which bars match, but the main problem is the different totals.
Counts are exact; they just depend on how many students each school has.
Right: counts grow with school size. Bar charts of relative frequencies would compare the schools fairly.
Bar charts of two different schools may not be compared
The schools may offer different subjects to their students
Counts are less accurate than relative frequencies are
The bigger school has taller bars even if its students choose subjects the same way

items.q: In a pie chart, a slice takes up a quarter of the circle. What percent of the individuals does it stand for?

why.correct: A slice is its category’s part of the whole: a quarter of the circle is $\frac{1}{4} = 25\%$.
options: The angle is 90 degrees out of 360, which is a quarter of the circle, so 25%.
Right: a quarter of the whole is 0.25, or 25%.
A quarter is one part of four, which is 1/4 = 25%.
One fourth is 0.25, not 0.40.
90%, from the slice’s angle of 90 degrees
4%, from the four quarters of the circle
40%, because a quarter is one fourth

items.q: Which feature does a bar chart need for its bar heights to compare values honestly? Select all that apply.

why.correct: The one requirement here is an axis that starts at 0; order, colors and gaps are design choices.
options: Right: heights are compared from 0, so the axis must start there.
Order is a free choice; it does not affect honesty.
Colors are a style choice; equal colors are just as honest.
Bars in a bar chart usually have gaps between them; touching is not required.
A vertical axis that starts at 0
Bars arranged in alphabetical order
A different color for each bar
Bars that touch each other

items.q: In a bar chart of how 80 students get to school, the tallest bar is "bus" at 34 students. What does this tell you?

why.correct: The tallest bar is the most common category, here bus with 34 of 80 students (42.5%).
options: 34 out of 80 is 0.425, less than half.
34 is a count; as a percent it is 34/80 = 42.5%.
The chart counts students; it says nothing about speed.
Right: the tallest bar marks the category with the largest count.
More than half of the 80 students ride the bus to school
Thirty-four percent of the 80 students ride the bus
The bus is faster than the other ways of getting to school
Bus is the most common way these students get to school

items.q: Two categories have relative frequencies 0.21 and 0.24. Which display makes their difference easier to see?

why.correct: Bar charts compare categories by length on one axis, which shows small differences better than slice angles do.
options: Right: the eye compares lengths on a common axis far better than the angles of slices.
Slices of 21% and 24% look almost the same; angles are hard to judge.
Lengths along a shared axis are easier to compare than slice angles.
It can be graphed; a bar chart shows it best.
A bar chart, since bars next to each other are easy to compare
A pie chart, since slices are easy to compare by their angles
Both displays make the difference equally easy to see
Neither display, as a difference this small is too hard to graph
